text: Two lads, two lovely little camping spots. One's got a view of the wheat and the silk, the other one's just looking at the rice, and I'll be honest, Paddy, he's looking at it hungrily. And tax? Reina, love, the desert doesn't pay the Emperor. The Emperor pays the desert, she just doesn't know it yet.
Rob stands his two soldiers on his desert: W1 on O18 (the notch where Provinces 5 and 7 meet) and W2 on T20 (just below Province 6). He says he won't pay tax.

Silke has the bank, Graham reads the card and gets his five a year, and Paddy collects, because nobody argues with a rice farmer holding a ledger. Forty percent, gentlemen, twenty-four apiece, and I'm building a palace with it. Rob, darling, I've written down every year you don't pay, and walls have long memories.

Reina names Silke banker, Graham card reader (5 a year from the crown, her choice) and Paddy tax collector. Year 1: no card; the 60 each player was dealt is the harvest. Tax at 40%: Paddy collects 24 each from Silke, Paddy and Graham, 72 to the crown; Rob doesn't pay. Reina builds the Summer Palace on F17 (20). The auctions follow: Silke's, then Paddy's, then Graham's.

One Dragon Jar, gentlemen, and only the one, so somebody goes home sad. Paddy, Graham, you both need it and you both know it. Six to open, and I'll be counting every grain into that Harvest Pile myself, honestly, since I'm the bank.
Silke puts up the Dragon Jar, the only one, minimum 6.

Graham, there's only the one jar, and if we go at each other over it the Harvest Pile eats us both. Let me have it near the six and you get first go at my Bamboo Brush at its minimum, no bid from me, my word on it in front of everyone. If not, well, I'm a rice farmer, I'm used to a long season.

Paddy. There's one jar and two of us, and every grain we throw at each other goes into Silke's pile, not our pockets. Stand aside on this one and my Vase is yours at the minimum when it comes up. Nobody bids against you, me included. That's the offer, and I'll say it once.

A Dragon Jar? In my desert? It'd just fill up with sand. No, you boys go on, fight over it, bid it up nice and high. Wherever it ends up, it'll be standing on a field, and I know where all the fields are.

The Dragon Jar goes to Paddy for 17: Graham bid up to 16, Rob passed. Silke keeps 4; 13 goes to the Harvest Pile. Paddy puts it on Q21. Paddy offered Graham first go at his Bamboo Brush at its minimum; Graham offered Paddy his Vase at the minimum. Next: Paddy's auction.

A promise is a promise, Graham, even if you made me pay seventeen for that jar. One Bamboo Brush, two to open, and I'll not bid a grain against you. Silke, there's another one coming next round, so maybe let the man have this one quiet.
Paddy puts up a Bamboo Brush (one of two), minimum 2, as he offered Graham.

Take it, Graham, I won't touch it. But everyone heard this: when the second Brush comes up, it's mine at the minimum. Graham won't need it by then, and Paddy, you'd be selling it to the woman who pays out your harvest.
Two. Thank you, Paddy. You kept your word, I'll give you that. Silke, there's a second one next round. I'd be grateful if you waited for it.
Look at this, honour among farmers. Lovely. Paddy, that's a handsome jar you've got sat out on Q21, by the way. Very shiny. You can see it from the desert.
Graham takes the Bamboo Brush at the minimum, 2 (Paddy keeps 0.5), and puts it on R14. Silke and Rob passed. Next: Graham's auction.

My offer on the Vase had a condition. Paddy, you were to stand aside on the jar, and you didn't, so that offer is gone. A Land Deed Scroll, two to open. There's one each for Silke and Paddy, so there's no need to fight over it.
Graham puts up a Land Deed Scroll (one of two), minimum 2. He keeps the Vase back.

There are two Scrolls and two of us, Paddy, so let's not feed the pile. I'll take this one at two, you take the next one at two, and I won't bid on yours. You've only got nineteen and a half left anyway, so save it for the Vase.

Fair enough, Graham, I did bid on the jar, I can't argue that. Silke, here's a deal for you: let me have this Scroll at two, and the second Brush is yours at the minimum next round, nobody else gets it, my word, same as I gave Graham. Then the second Scroll's yours and nobody's out of pocket.

Oh, Graham's cross with Paddy, Silke's cross with Graham, and Paddy's down to his last nineteen and a half. Isn't this a happy table? Go on, sell your scrolls. I'm not bidding, I'm just enjoying the show.
Grand, Silke, it's yours, and I'll hold you to the other half: the next Scroll's mine at two and you keep your hands in your pockets. Everyone heard it.

Silke takes the Land Deed Scroll for 5 (Paddy went to 4, then passed; Rob passed). Graham keeps 1; 4 to the Harvest Pile. Silke puts it on O22. Paddy and Silke agree in public: the second Scroll to Paddy at 2, the second Brush to Silke at the minimum. The auctions are over; Rob marches.

To correct the last line: Paddy offered Silke the second Brush at the minimum in return for this Scroll, which went to Silke. What stands, as talk, is Silke's word that she won't bid on the second Scroll.
Morning, Silke. Morning, Paddy. That'll be five each, thank you, call it a visitor's fee. And Graham, don't feel left out, I've just hired a nice young man to stand at the bottom of your garden.

Rob marches: W1 steps onto O19 and raids Silke's Province 5 (5 from Silke); W2 steps onto S21 and raids Paddy's Province 6 (5 from Paddy). He hires a third soldier, W3, for 20 (to the Harvest Pile) on T14, two squares below Graham's Brush; it moves from next year. Provinces 5 and 6 have now been raided, so any soldier bought there may move. Reina pays Graham his 5. End of Year 1: Reina 107, Silke 30, Paddy 14.5, Graham 40, Rob 50.

Year 2. Graham turns the first card: The Canal Gives Way. An average harvest everywhere (no canal is dug, so none is lost). Silke pays out the harvest: Reina +15, each peasant +35, Rob +10. Graham and Rob play a personal disaster: Graham's hail costs him 2; Rob is wounded in the legs, so no raids on Provinces 5, 6 or 7 this year.
A correction to your last prompt: W1 on O19 is 5 rounds from J23, the nearest square of Province 1, not 4.

Forty percent again, friends. I said steady and I meant it, so nobody at this table gets surprised by me. And the crown is digging a canal this year. Rob, I hear you've hurt your legs. Rest them. It's a long walk to Province 1.

Year 2 tax at 40%: Paddy collects 14 each from Silke, Paddy and Graham, 42 to the crown; Rob doesn't pay. Reina digs the first Grand Canal section in Province 1 (40); it adds 10 to her harvest from next year. The auctions follow: Silke's, Paddy's, Graham's.

One Customs House, two to open. There's one for each of you, boys, so there's nothing to fight over. I'm keeping it cheap because I've got a long memory too, Reina, and I'd like these two to remember who was kind to them when the Vase and the Bowl come round.
For the record: Paddy's offer of his second Brush at the minimum was in return for the first Scroll, which you won; as things stand he owes you nothing on it.
Silke puts up a Customs House (one of two), minimum 2.

Thank you, Silke, that's kindly done. Graham, I know I owe you one after the jar, so here's the fairest deal I can make: there are two Houses, so let me have this one at two and I won't bid a grain on the second. Or if you'd rather have this one, say so now and I'll wait for the next. Either way neither of us feeds the pile.
Thank you, Silke. Paddy, there are two of these. I'll take this one cheap, and I won't bid on the next.
Bad legs, Reina, not a bad memory. I'll rest them this year, and so will you all, I expect. Enjoy it. Customs House? Nothing to declare, Silke, I'm sat in the sand.
Take it at six, Paddy. Everyone heard you: you won't bid a grain on the second one. I'll be counting.

Paddy takes the Customs House at 6: he and Graham both stopped at 6, the tie went to the earlier seat, and Graham passed on a raise. Silke keeps 1.5; 4.5 to the Harvest Pile. Paddy puts it on Q24. Next: Paddy's auction.

The Wooden Bowl, friends, the only one in China, four to open. Silke, Graham, you both need it, so I'll leave it to the two of you, and you'd do well to settle it between you before you start feeding the pile. Silke, the Brush comes next year, and it's yours at the minimum, same as I said.
Paddy puts up the Wooden Bowl, the only one, minimum 4. Silke and Graham both need it.

Graham, I'm the only one in China with a Customs House left, and I set its minimum. Stand aside on the Bowl and it's yours next year at two, my word, in front of everyone. If you bid against me here, don't be surprised when that minimum turns out to be twenty.

Silke. You need the Vase, and I'm the only one who has it. Stand aside on this Bowl and the Vase is yours next round at the minimum, and I'll keep Paddy off it. This offer has a condition too, and I'll hold you to it exactly.
The only bowl in all of China, and two hungry farmers. Silke, Graham, settle it nicely or don't, I'm easy either way. Whoever gets it, put it somewhere pretty. Somewhere close to the edge, ideally.

Your Vase is no good to me without the Bowl, Graham, and you know it, so that offer was empty. Twenty-five. Every grain past this goes into the pile I pay out, so keep going if you like feeding Rob's harvest.
Twenty-five. Take it, Silke. And you're right, the Vase is no good to you without the Bowl. Now that you have the Bowl, it's no good to you without the Vase. Next round, we'll see what it's worth.
Silke takes the Wooden Bowl for 25: Graham led at 21, Silke came back with 25, Graham passed. Paddy keeps 6; 19 to the Harvest Pile. Silke puts it on O23. Next: Graham's auction.

My last Land Deed Scroll, two to open. Paddy, that's yours, and Silke has already given her word she won't bid. The Vase comes next year. Silke, your Customs House goes up before my Vase does. Set its minimum however you like. I'll be setting mine afterwards.
Graham puts up his last Land Deed Scroll, minimum 2. The Vase, the last piece in his stock, will go up next year.

I gave my word, so it's Paddy's. Graham, you need my Customs House and I need your Vase, and we're the only seller of each. Both at two next year, in front of everyone. Or we can both set them at thirty and let Rob laugh at us.
Thank you, Graham, that's decent of you, and I'll not forget it. Two it is, and if anyone fancies bidding it up just to watch me sweat, you'll only be feeding the pile.
Twenty-five for a bowl. Silke, I'm touched, honestly. Half of that's going into the Harvest Pile, and the harvest pays me too. Go on, Paddy, take your scroll. I'm not in the paperwork business.
Rob said half of Silke's 25 went to the Harvest Pile: it was 19 (three quarters, rounded in the seller's favour); Paddy kept 6.

Paddy takes Graham's last Land Deed Scroll at the minimum, 2 (Graham keeps 0.5), and puts it on Q25. Silke and Rob passed. Paddy now holds the Jar, a Customs House and a Scroll; he needs only the Vase. The auctions are over; Rob marches (no raids on Provinces 5, 6 or 7 this year).
Silke has two pieces on row O, the Scroll on O22 and the Bowl on O23; W1 on O19 is 3 rounds from O22 and 4 from O23.

The lads are resting their legs, just like Her Majesty told them to. Sitting on your doorsteps, Silke, Paddy, Graham, enjoying the view. Don't mind them, they'll be gone soon enough, and something of yours will go with them.
Rob's soldiers all stand still (W1 O19, W2 S21, W3 T14). Reina pays Graham his 5. End of Year 2: Reina 119, Silke 27.5, Paddy 33.5, Graham 64.5, Rob 60.

Year 3. Graham turns the card: Population Grows by Half. A good harvest everywhere, and from now on every province eats half as much again (a peasant 60, the Emperor 90, the Warlord 30). The harvest is paid: Silke, Paddy and Graham +40 each, Reina +20 (her canal's 10 included), Rob +10. Grain now: Reina 139, Silke 67.5, Paddy 73.5, Graham 104.5, Rob 70.

Forty percent again, my dears, same as the last two years, so nobody here gets surprised by me, even with more mouths to feed. The Winter Palace goes up on G18 this year, and after that the canals come down the coast to Silke and Paddy. Rob, darling, that's year three you haven't paid. I've written it down.

Year 3 tax at 40%: Paddy collects 16 each from Silke, Paddy and Graham, 48 to the crown; Rob doesn't pay. Reina builds the Winter Palace on G18 (20); the Grand Canal may now be dug in Provinces 5 and 6. 440 of the works still owed. The auctions follow: Silke's, Paddy's, Graham's.
From the record: at Year 2's Bowl auction (023) Paddy said, 'Silke, the Brush comes next year, and it's yours at the minimum, same as I said.' He hasn't taken it back at the table since.

Two, Graham, like I promised. I said both at two, and I've done my half in front of everyone, so Reina can write it down. Your Vase comes up after Paddy's Brush, and the whole table will be watching to see whether a Garner keeps a deal as well as a Weber does. Paddy, you're welcome to bid on my Customs House, but you've already got one and it'd only be feeding Rob's pile.
Silke puts up her last Customs House, minimum 2. Only Graham still needs one; Paddy already holds one.
I said I'd keep off Silke's Customs House and I will. It's yours, Graham, at two, and good luck to you. And Graham, I know I owe you one for the Jar. I haven't forgotten it.
Two, then. Thank you, Silke. I'll note that you kept it. Paddy, I've noted yours too. The Vase comes up after the Brush, and it'll go up at the price that was agreed.
Look at that. Three farmers, one customs house, and nobody's thrown the bowl yet. I'm almost proud of you. Go on, Graham, have it for two. That leaves you a bit more to spare for my visitor's fee.

Graham takes Silke's last Customs House at the minimum, 2 (Silke keeps 0.5; 1.5 to the Harvest Pile), and puts it on Q15. Paddy and Rob passed. Graham now holds a Brush and a Customs House; he still needs the Jar and the Bowl. Next: Paddy's auction, his last Bamboo Brush.
Graham has 88.5 grain to your 70; Reina has 167.

Two, Silke, like I promised last year. A Doyle keeps his word as well as a Weber or a Garner does. Graham, when your Vase comes up I'll bid on it honestly and in the open, and whatever happens there'll be no hard feelings from me.
Paddy puts up his last Bamboo Brush, minimum 2. Only Silke still needs one; Graham already holds his.

Two, and thank you, Paddy. You said it last year and you kept it, and I'll say so to anyone who asks. Rob, if you want to bid on a brush you've no use for, go ahead, but every grain you put in goes to the Harvest Pile and not to you.
I've got a brush already, so I'll stay out of it. Silke kept her word on the Customs House and I'm not going to push up the price of hers. The Vase is next.
Relax, Silke, I don't write letters. Have your brush for two. Mind you, it's a lovely thing to own, and a lovely thing to lose.

Silke takes Paddy's last Bamboo Brush at the minimum, 2 (Paddy keeps 0.5; 1.5 to the Harvest Pile), and puts it on O25. Graham and Rob passed. Silke now holds the Scroll, the Bowl and the Brush; she needs only the Vase. Paddy needs only the Vase too. Next: Graham's auction, the Vase, the last piece in his stock.
Two, the price Silke and I agreed. A Garner keeps his word, so you can write that down as well, Reina. I promised the minimum, nothing more, so the two of you can settle the rest between you.
Graham puts up the Vase, the only one, minimum 2. Silke and Paddy each need only the Vase; whoever buys it holds a complete set.

Paddy, last year I stood aside on the Scroll so you could have it at two, and the whole table watched me do it. I'm asking you to do the same for me now. If we fight over it, every grain we bid goes into the pile and Rob gets to watch two farmers ruin each other over one pot.

Silke, I won't pretend I didn't notice you standing aside on that Scroll. But you'd already got a Scroll of your own on O22, so it cost you nothing, and this pot is the whole game for both of us. I can't give you the whole game for a favour like that. I'll bid fair and in the open, and whoever ends up with the Vase, the other one shakes hands on it.

Oh, don't mind me, I've got the best seat in the house. Two farmers, one pot, and the whole game riding on it. Go on, Paddy, Silke, bid like you mean it. Every grain you throw in is one less you can use to buy off my lads.

Paddy takes the Vase for 29: Silke stopped at 28. Rob passed. Graham keeps 7; 22 to the Harvest Pile. Paddy puts it on S24. He now holds the Jar, a Customs House, a Scroll and the Vase, and 29 grain: a complete set.
Take it, Paddy. And remember I'm the one who held the bank while you did it.

Silke, I'm sorry, truly I am, but I'll be taking the Silk province now. You'll have sixty grain and my old rice fields, and they're good fields, I promise you. They've been kind to me. Rob, your lads can have a look at Province 6 if they like, but I won't be there.

Paddy shows his complete set and his 20 and replaces Silke as the Silk Peasant in Province 5. He takes her 50 on top of his 29 (79 now) and keeps the Customs House, the Scroll and the Vase, placed on O22, O23 and O24; the Dragon Jar, Province 5's own piece, goes into his stock for next year's auction. Silke returns her Scroll, Bowl and Brush, draws 60 from the Harvest Pile, and is now the Rice Peasant in Province 6. Her Bowl and Brush go into Province 6's stock (hers to sell from next year); her Scroll goes into Graham's stock. Paddy drew seat 6 and now holds seat 5.

You are now the Rice Peasant, Province 6 (the south-east coast), with 60 grain and no realia on the board. Your stock: the Wooden Bowl and a Bamboo Brush, to auction one a year from next year. As the Rice Peasant you need a Customs House, a Land Deed Scroll, the Vase and the Dragon Jar, and 20 grain, to change places with the Official, the Scholar or another peasant (seats 2-4 are empty here, so: Paddy or Graham).

You are now the Silk Peasant, Province 5 (the east coast). As the Silk Peasant you need a Land Deed Scroll, a Bamboo Brush, the Vase and the Wooden Bowl, and 20 grain, to change places again (with Graham or Silke; seats 2-4 are empty here). Your stock: the Dragon Jar, to auction next year.

Congratulations, Paddy, a full set and a new house on the coast! Shame you've put every piece you own in one tidy row on O22, O23 and O24. I'll be round with a housewarming present. Silke, love, welcome to the rice fields. Visitor's fee's five, same as it ever was. Graham, keep that brush polished, my lad's nearly at your gate.

Rob marches: W1 to O20 (raids Paddy's Province 5, 5), W2 to R22 (raids Silke's Province 6, 5), W3 to S14 (raids Graham's Province 7, 5, its first raid). No hire. Now W1 is 2 from Paddy's Customs House on O22, and W3 is 1 from Graham's Brush on R14 and 2 from his Customs House on Q15. Reina pays Graham his 5. End of Year 3: Reina 162, Silke 55, Paddy 74, Graham 93.5, Rob 85.

Year 4. Graham turns the card: Bad Harvest. Every province eats more than it grows: Silke, Paddy, Graham and Rob each pay 10 into the Harvest Pile, Reina 30 (her canal's 10 included). Grain now: Reina 132, Silke 45, Paddy 64, Graham 83.5, Rob 75.

Forty percent, as always. It's worth nothing in a year like this, but I said the rate wouldn't move, and it won't. I'm digging my own second canal section with my own grain. Congratulations on the coast, Paddy. Silke, the rice fields will treat you well. Rob, darling, that's year four on the tally.

Year 4 tax at 40%: every income is negative, so nothing is owed and nothing collected. Reina digs Province 1's second Grand Canal section (40); it adds another 10 to her harvest from next year. 400 of the works still owed. The auctions follow, in province order: Paddy's (5), Silke's (6), Graham's (7).

Two, and that's all I'm asking. Silke, Graham, you both need it, so settle it between you however you think is fair. I'd rather it went cheap than see half the jar go into the Harvest Pile over a quarrel. Silke, I haven't forgotten you held the bank for me. And Rob, you'll get no housewarming fee out of me if I can help it.
Paddy puts up the Dragon Jar, the only one, minimum 2. Graham and Silke both need it.
At auction three quarters of the price goes to the Harvest Pile (less the seller's rounding), not half; the seller keeps a quarter.

Graham, before you bid, I've got the only Wooden Bowl in China in my stock now, and you can't finish without it. Let me have this Jar at two and the Bowl goes up at two next year, my word in front of Reina's book. Bid me up on it, and the Bowl's minimum will be whatever you've got left.

Silke, there's one Vase in China and it's on Paddy's square at O24. Without it a jar is no use to you, it's just a pot. I'm bidding for it, and I'll bid all the way. When your Bowl comes up, set any minimum you like, and the table can watch you charge me for a set you'll never finish.

Here we go again, another year and another pot to fight over. Graham's going to bid all the way, Silke's going to set the bowl at whatever he's got left, and Paddy sits on the coast saying 'settle it fairly.' Lovely stuff. Paddy, love, about that housewarming fee: my lad on O20 is two steps from your front door, and he's never needed an invitation.
Keep it, Graham. Just remember who's selling the Bowl next year.

Graham takes the Dragon Jar for 23: Silke stopped at 22. Rob passed. Paddy keeps 5.5; 17.5 to the Harvest Pile. Graham puts it on P15. He now holds the Brush, a Customs House and the Jar; he needs only the Wooden Bowl, which is in Silke's stock. Next: Silke's auction, the Bowl or the Brush.
Every province paid into the Harvest Pile at this year's bad harvest, Rob included (10).

The Brush, at two. Paddy let me have one at two last year, so that's him paid back in kind. Graham, the Bowl comes up next year. Your Scroll comes up in a minute, so set it at two and the Bowl goes up at two, your word for my word. Set it high and you'll find out exactly how long a year is.
Silke puts up the Bamboo Brush, minimum 2, and keeps the Wooden Bowl back for next year. Only Paddy needs a Brush.

Thank you, Silke, that's a kind turn, and I'll take it at two if nobody minds. You and I are square now on brushes. Rob, if you want to bid on a brush you can't use, go ahead, but you'll only be paying the Harvest Pile for the pleasure.

The brush is yours, Paddy, I'll stay out of it. Silke, I'll take that deal: my Scroll at two now, your Bowl at two next year, in front of Reina's book. I kept the last one we made, so check the list if you doubt me.

Have it, Paddy, you're right, I can't paint. Look at the three of you, though, all square and shaking hands and writing everything in Reina's book. Graham, you're one bowl short now, and you've got your jar, your brush and your customs house all sitting in a row on P15, Q15 and R14. That's a lovely little shop window for my lad on S14.

Paddy takes Silke's Bamboo Brush at the minimum, 2 (Silke keeps 0.5; 1.5 to the Harvest Pile), and puts it on P25. Graham and Rob passed. Paddy now holds a Customs House, the Scroll, the Vase and the Brush: like Graham, he needs only the Wooden Bowl, the last piece in Silke's stock, which must go up next year. Next: Graham's auction, his Land Deed Scroll.

Two, Silke, as we agreed, and Reina has it in her book. Paddy, I see you need the Bowl now as well. Our deal sets the minimum at two, but it can't stop anyone bidding, so when it comes up I'll be bidding against you in the open, the same as you did to me over the Vase.
Graham puts up the Land Deed Scroll, minimum 2. Only Silke needs one.
From the record: over the Vase (Year 3) Graham was the seller and Paddy bid against Silke; it was the Jar and the Customs House (Years 1-2) that Paddy won against Graham.

It's Silke's scroll, I've already got one. And Graham, so you can stop fretting, I'll stay out of that Bowl next year. A full set wouldn't do me any good, since the only seats I could swap into are further down the coast than the one I've got. It's between you and Silke, and you've already made your deal.

Two it is, Graham, and the Bowl goes up at two next year, I'm not taking that back. And thank you, Paddy, for standing out of it. Mind you, Graham, Reina's book has you down for the Vase, not Paddy. Paddy bid against me, not against you. Let's keep the record straight if we're all going to swear by it.

Go on, Silke, take it for two. Get something back on the board, love, you've had nothing out there since Paddy moved in on your coast. Listen to the three of you, correcting each other's minutes. You'll be electing a chairman next.

Silke takes Graham's Land Deed Scroll at the minimum, 2 (Graham keeps 0.5; 1.5 to the Harvest Pile), and puts it on Q25. Paddy and Rob passed. The auctions are over: only the Wooden Bowl is left beside the board, in Silke's stock, to go up next year. Rob marches.

Graham, my lad's just come through your garden gate and he's very taken with your brush. He'll be keeping it. Paddy, he's one step from your customs house now, so put the kettle on. And Silke, lovely scroll, that. It'd look even better in the desert.

Rob marches: W3 steps onto R14 and takes Graham's Bamboo Brush, his first raided piece (it goes onto his desert at T14). W1 steps onto O21 (raids Paddy, 5); W2 onto Q23 (raids Silke, 5). Now W1 is 1 from Paddy's Customs House on O22 and W2 is 2 from Silke's Scroll on Q25. Graham now needs the Brush and the Bowl. Reina pays Graham his 5. End of Year 4: Reina 87, Silke 38.5, Paddy 62.5, Graham 66, Rob 85.

A new table ruling from Manish, taking effect now: with no Official, Gentry or Scholar at this table, the Silk Peasant stands in for the upper class. A Silk Peasant who completes the Silk set (a Scroll, a Brush, the Vase and the Bowl) and holds 20 grain may take the throne. The Silk Peasant returns their realia; the Emperor hands over the whole reserve, draws 60 from the Harvest Pile and takes the Silk seat. The Rice and Wheat Peasants still climb to Silk first, and either may go straight there.

Year 5 begins. Graham turns the I Ching card: Population Grows by Half. The villages have already grown by half once, so only the good harvest counts. Silke pays out the harvest: Reina 117, Silke 78.5, Paddy 102.5, Graham 106, Rob 95.

Storyteller's note, the true board at the start of Year 5 (some diaries were written before the last news of Year 4): Rob's W3 took Graham's Bamboo Brush from R14 and it stands on Rob's desert at T14; W1 stands on O21, one square from Paddy's Customs House on O22; W2 stands on Q23, two from Silke's Scroll on Q25. The only piece left beside the board is Silke's Wooden Bowl, which must go up this year. Your board card has everyone's grain.

Forty percent, five years running. Write it down, Silke. The canal goes down the coast as I promised, and it starts in the rice fields, because the rice fields have had the worst of it. And Paddy, my dear, you told this whole table you'd stay out of the Bowl, and that's in my book too. I'll only say that if anyone at this table bids on that Bowl to get a seat they never mentioned, they'll find the Emperor bidding against them, and I have the deepest pockets in China. Rob, darling, you're refusing again, I assume? Year five on the tally.

Year 5 tax at 40%: Paddy collects 16 each from Silke, Paddy and Graham, 48 to the crown; Rob doesn't pay. Reina digs the first Grand Canal section in Province 6, Silke's (40, paid into the Harvest Pile); it adds 10 to Silke's harvest from next year. 360 of the works still owed. Grain now: Reina 125, Silke 62.5, Paddy 86.5, Graham 90, Rob 95. The auction follows: only Silke has stock, the Wooden Bowl.
From the rules: the Emperor may not bid at auction (Section 10). Rob may.

Two. I said two when Graham gave me his Scroll, and I said I wasn't taking it back, so I'm not. Paddy, you told the whole table you'd stay out of this Bowl, and now the Bowl is a throne. And Reina, Section 10 says you can't bid, so all that's guarding your seat now is Paddy's word. Let's find out what it's worth.

Silke puts up the Wooden Bowl, the only one, at the minimum, 2, as she promised Graham. Paddy needs it for the last piece of his Silk set (with it and 20 grain he may take the throne); Graham needs it too, and a Brush.

I said I'd stay out of the Bowl, and I meant it when I said it, so I'm staying out of it. I know what it's worth now, Silke, you needn't tell me. But a man who breaks his word the minute it gets expensive was never worth the trust in the first place. Graham, it's yours at two if nobody else wants it, and good luck to you. Next year's another year, though, and I never promised anything about next year.
Paddy passes on the Bowl.

Silke's right, and I'll take the correction: the Vase was Paddy against her, not Paddy against me. I'll fix my list tonight. Two is what we agreed, Silke, and thank you, Paddy. I'll remember that you said it and then did it. Rob, if your man fancies a bowl as well, he'll be paying a lot more than two for it.
Graham bids.

Pass, five years running, Reina, write it down next to the tax. I don't buy pots, Graham, I collect them. Two grain for the only bowl in China, and Paddy keeping his word in public? I'd like that in the committee's minutes, please, before somebody corrects them.

Graham takes the Wooden Bowl at the minimum, 2 (Silke keeps 0.5; 1.5 to the Harvest Pile), and puts it on P17. Paddy and Rob passed. Graham holds a Customs House, the Jar and the Bowl; he still needs a Brush (Paddy's is on P25; the one Rob took is on Rob's desert at T14). Every piece is now sold. Rob marches.

Paddy, your customs house is under new management, and my man's very good with paperwork. Silke, that's five for the visitor's fee, and the scroll's next on his list. Graham, congratulations on the bowl. My lad's just come to admire it and leave a small bill.

Rob marches: W1 steps onto O22 and takes Paddy's Customs House, his second raided piece (it goes onto his desert at O18). W2 steps onto Q24 (raids Silke, 5); W3 onto R15 (raids Graham, 5). Paddy now holds the Scroll, the Vase and a Brush, and needs a Customs House again; both Customs Houses are on the board (Graham's on Q15, Rob's on O18). Reina pays Graham his 5. End of Year 5: Reina 120, Silke 58, Paddy 86.5, Graham 88, Rob 105.

Year 6 begins. Graham turns the I Ching card: Population Doubles. A good harvest, but every province now eats twice what it ate, so every province eats more than it grows: Reina -60, Silke -10 (her new canal helps), Paddy, Graham and Rob -20 each. New harvest squares may now be bought. Grain: Reina 60, Silke 48, Paddy 66.5, Graham 68, Rob 85.
Correction: Paddy, as the Silk Peasant, needs no Customs House. He holds the Scroll, the Vase and a Brush, and needs only the Bowl, which Graham holds.

Forty percent, six years running, and yes, Silke, it raises nothing, and yes, it's in the book anyway. The crown ate sixty this year, the same as all of you went hungry, so no works and no spending until the granary fills again. Graham, your five is suspended for one lean year, not cancelled, and I'll pay it back when the harvest turns. Anyone who buys new land gets five a square from me, and that's the whole of my charity. Rob, darling, year six on the tally.

Year 6 tax at 40%: every income is negative, so nothing is owed or collected. No public work this year; 360 of the works still owed. Reina offers 5 a square toward any peasant's new land, and suspends Graham's 5 for this year. There are no auctions: every piece has been sold.

My promise was for Year 5, and I kept it to the letter. You all saw me do it. So here it is in the open, Graham: forty grain for your Bowl, today. That's twenty times what you paid. You need a Brush to finish, and there are only two in China, mine and the one in Rob's desert, so that Bowl's worth more to me than it'll ever be to you. Reina, I'm sorry, but I did say next year was another year.
Paddy offers Graham 40 grain for the Wooden Bowl, paid at once if Graham agrees. He buys no land and no soldier. Graham will answer on his turn, after Silke's.

Rob, I'll have one of your lads, and he'll be standing on my scroll, so yours can come and knock if he likes. And Graham, forty's a lovely number, but you're not selling Paddy a bowl, you're selling him the throne. Ask yourself what the Emperor charges the man who sold it to him.
Silke buys a soldier from Rob (20; Rob keeps 5, 15 to the Harvest Pile) and stands it on Q25, on her Land Deed Scroll, to guard it. Rob's W2 stands beside it on Q24. Silke has 28 grain, Rob 90.

No, Paddy. You kept your word for exactly one year and I've written down that you did, but the Bowl isn't for sale at forty or at any price. Rob, you said you collect pots and don't buy them. Then sell me one back: thirty grain, today, for the brush your lad took off my garden. That's more than anyone at this table has ever paid you for a raid.

Graham refuses Paddy's offer for the Bowl. He offers Rob 30 grain for the Bamboo Brush on Rob's desert at T14 (the one Rob's soldier took from him), paid at once, to go on P18. No land, no soldier. Rob answers before he marches.

Thirty, Graham? Done. I did say it was a lovely thing to own and a lovely thing to lose, and I never said who'd be losing it. Silke, your lad's a credit to you, he stood his ground beautifully and now he works for me. And Paddy, your scroll's coming for a little walk in the desert, so do please correct the committee's minutes.

Rob accepts: Graham pays him 30 and the Bamboo Brush goes from Rob's desert to Graham's P18. Graham now holds a complete Wheat set (Customs House, Brush, Jar, Bowl). Then Rob marches: W2 steps straight onto Q25, captures Silke's soldier and takes Silke's Land Deed Scroll (to his desert at T24), his third raided piece: one from each of Graham, Paddy and Silke, so Rob's objective is complete. W1 steps onto O23 and takes Paddy's Land Deed Scroll (to N18). W3 steps onto Q16 and raids Graham, 5. Grain: Reina 60, Silke 28, Paddy 66.5, Graham 33, Rob 125. Paddy holds the Vase and a Brush; Silke holds nothing.

I'm taking the silk coast, Paddy. Silke kept every promise she made me, so I won't be the one who sends her inland. You told us next year was another year, and this is it. The Jar goes up for auction next year, and anyone who wants it can bid in the open. That's how I've played it all game.

Graham replaces Paddy as the Silk Peasant (Province 5), with 99.5 grain (his 33 and Paddy's 66.5). The Dragon Jar, Province 5's own piece, goes back into the Silk stock for Graham to auction; his Customs House, Brush and Bowl stand on P19, P20 and N20. Paddy returns his Vase (into the Wheat stock) and his Brush (into the Rice stock), draws 60 from the pile and becomes the Wheat Peasant (Province 7). Rob, whose objective is complete, decides next whether to change seats.

Reina, darling, six years you kept a tally of my sins, so you'll know exactly where you put the book. Pass it here, and the keys to the Winter Palace while you're at it. Walls have long memories, you said. Let's see how long they are from the other side. The desert's yours now, and the lads are good boys, they only need feeding.

Rob takes the throne. He returns his pieces for auction (the Customs House into Graham's Silk stock, both Scrolls into Paddy's Wheat stock) and takes Reina's whole reserve: Emperor Rob has 185. Reina draws 60 from the pile and becomes the Warlord, with W1 on O23, W2 on Q25 and W3 on Q16. The table jobs stay: Silke banker, Graham card reader, Paddy tax collector; no salaries this year. End of Year 6. Seats: Rob Emperor (1), Graham Silk (5), Silke Rice (6), Paddy Wheat (7), Reina Warlord (8). Grain: Rob 185, Graham 99.5, Reina 60, Paddy 60, Silke 28. Beside the board, to be auctioned: Graham's stock, the Dragon Jar and a Customs House; Silke's, a Brush; Paddy's, the Vase and two Scrolls. Graham holds a Customs House (P19), a Brush (P20) and the Bowl (N20).
The Harvest Pile isn't the Emperor's: three quarters of every auction price goes to the pile, which pays the harvests; the crown's income is the tax and its own harvest.
Your Warlord card's objective line still lists the pieces Rob raided; whether a new Warlord's count starts afresh is a ruling still to come. Your soldiers are W1 O23, W2 Q25, W3 Q16.

Well, that's the year. Committee, the minutes will now show that the desert has a throne and the throne has a book. Reina, my love, the lads like their rations on time, and they don't care for long speeches about walls. Same tax rate as before, I'm told, so nobody can say I'm not a traditionalist.

Emperor Rob. I've had three different seats in six years, and each one cost less than the last. Paddy, the Vase and both Scrolls are in your stock now, so we'll have something to talk about next year. I'll keep it in the open, the way you did with the Bowl.

Twenty-eight grain, no pieces, and the man who took my scroll now owns the book that recorded it. Fine. Graham, thank you for keeping me on the coast; I'll remember it. Rob, Your Majesty, I'm still the banker, so every grain you hand out goes through my hands first.

Well. I came here a rice farmer and I'm going home a wheat farmer with sixty grain and an empty field, so I suppose that's a step up. Fair play to you, Graham. You did it in the open and I can't fault you for that. Rob, God help us all. Reina, if those lads of yours need feeding, I've a Vase and two Scrolls to sell next year, and I'm not proud.

Take the book, darling, it's all in there, and you'll find your tally runs out at year six. Mine starts at year seven. Enjoy the Winter Palace, Rob. Three hundred and sixty in works still owed, a population that's just doubled, and an empty Province 1 under a wall nobody's finished. I built you a lovely house. Now you get to pay for the rest of the street.

A table ruling from Manish, taking effect now: a new Warlord keeps the army where it stands and starts the objective afresh. Reina commands W1, W2 and W3; only raids she makes herself count. Her targets are Graham, Silke and Paddy (every other realia-holding seat); the Emperor is still left out, so Rob is safe while he holds the throne.
Graham turns the I Ching card: Bad Harvest. Every province collects a bad harvest, and with the population doubled every province eats more than it grows.

Harvest: every province pays the pile. Rob -110 (75 left), Graham -70 (29.5), Paddy -70 (10 in debt), Silke -60 (her canal earns her 10; 32 in debt), Reina -40 (20). Silke and Paddy hold no piece on the board to sell back, so they are in debt: until it's paid they can't bid, buy, trade, give grain or change seats, and every grain they receive (an auction commission included) pays the debt first. A player in debt is a cause for revolt (two other players must agree).

Right, committee, take this down. Tax stays the same, because I'm a traditionalist and because there's nothing to tax. The Emperor will now pay for something with his own grain, which I appreciate is a shock to everyone at this table, me included. Silke, that's your canal finished, forty grain, and it all goes through your hands, as you so kindly reminded me. Graham, you're still reading the cards and I'm paying you five for it, because I'd like at least one of you to be able to afford a cup of tea. Paddy, the Reservoir's there next year if you can stay out of trouble. Lovely thing to own, a canal. Very hard to start a revolt about.

Tax 40%, raising nothing (every income is negative). Rob builds the second and last Grand Canal section in Province 6 (Silke's) for 40 from his own grain: +10 to Silke's harvest from next year; 320 of the works still owed. Rob keeps the jobs and will pay Graham his 5. Rob 35.

The Customs House, at two. Reina, you're the only one at this table who can lift a hand, so it's yours at two if you want a building in the sand. I'm keeping the Jar. Paddy, once you're out of the red, the Jar's on the table for a Scroll, straight swap, and I'll say that again next year in front of everyone.
Graham puts up his spare Customs House, minimum 2, and keeps the Dragon Jar back for next year. Only Reina may bid: Silke and Paddy are in debt, and the Emperor doesn't bid.
Two grain for a house in the sand, Graham? Sold, darling. I've built palaces for less gratitude. Rob, write it in the book: the desert now has a building and a throne, and only one of those is mine.
Reina takes the Customs House at 2 and stands it on her desert at O18 (it counts nothing toward her objective). Graham keeps 0.5; 1.5 to the Harvest Pile.

The only Brush in the Rice stock, minimum fifteen. Reina, it's no use to you in the sand, and Graham, you've got one already, so if either of you pays fifteen just to keep it away from Paddy, everyone at this table will know exactly why you did it. Otherwise it stays with me until Paddy's out of the red, and then he and I will talk.
Silke puts up the Bamboo Brush, minimum 15. Only Graham and Reina may bid. If nobody bids, it stays in her stock and must go up again next year.
I've got a brush already, Silke, and I paid for it twice. I'm not paying fifteen for a third one just to make a point. Paddy can have it when he's back on his feet.
Fifteen for a brush I'd only use to sweep sand? No, Silke, keep it for Paddy. I'd much rather see it planted in his wheat field where everyone can admire it.
Graham and Reina pass. Nobody bids, so the Bamboo Brush stays in Silke's stock and goes up again next year.

One Scroll, lads, minimum ten. The Vase stays with me until Silke can bid on it as well. It wouldn't be fair to sell the only one while half the table has its hands tied, and I'm not going to start doing things unfairly now I'm the one in the red. Graham, I heard you about the Jar for my other Scroll. I'll hold you to it in front of everyone the day I'm square.
Paddy puts up a Land Deed Scroll, minimum 10, and keeps the Vase and his other Scroll in stock. Only Graham and Reina may bid.
Ten for the Scroll, Paddy, at your price, and thank you for not making the Vase a race nobody else can run. Reina, a land deed's no use in the desert. There's no land out there to deed.

A land deed in the desert, Paddy? I hold the whole desert already and nobody's ever asked to see the paperwork. Graham, it's yours if you want it. Just don't stand it too far from my lads, they get lonely.

Graham takes the Land Deed Scroll at 10 and puts it on L24. Paddy keeps 2.5, which pays his debt down to 7.5. Graham now holds a Customs House, a Brush, the Bowl and a Scroll, with 20 grain: for the Silk set, and the throne, he needs only the Vase, still in Paddy's stock.

Paddy, darling, you offered to feed my lads, and they've taken you at your word. Five from the wheat fields, and I'll remember the kindness. Graham, don't look so worried. Nobody's walking to the coast this year. Probably.
Reina marches: W3 steps onto P17 and raids Paddy's Province 7 for 5 (his debt is now 12.5). W1 steps onto N22 in empty Province 4 and W2 onto Q24, already raided; neither raids. No hire.

Salaries: Rob pays Graham his 5 for reading the cards. End of Year 7. Grain: Rob 30, Graham 25, Reina 23, Paddy -12.5, Silke -32. Graham needs only the Vase for the Silk set. Beside the board: the Dragon Jar (Graham), the Brush (Silke), the Vase and a Scroll (Paddy).

Year 8. Graham turns the I Ching card: The Emperor's Share. Every province collects an average harvest, and every province with a public work splits the extra harvest it produces 50/50 with the Emperor. Every province eats more than it grows: Rob -85, Graham -45, Paddy -45, Reina -30, Silke -25 (her canal earns her 20).

Sell before you sink: Graham had 25 and owed 45, so he sells all four of his pieces (Customs House, Bamboo Brush, Wooden Bowl, Land Deed Scroll) back to the Harvest Pile at 2 each, 8 in all; they go into the pile's own stock, to be auctioned after the provinces' lots. Reina sells her Customs House from O18 back for 2. Silke pays Rob his share, 10 (half her canal's 20).

Every player is now in debt to the pile: Rob 45, Graham 12, Reina 5, Paddy 57.5, Silke 67. Nothing stands on the board. In debt nobody may bid, buy, trade, give grain, pay toward a public work or change seats, and every grain received pays the debt first. Debt is a cause for revolt (two other players must agree).

Well, committee, the minutes will show that for the first time in eight years this table is in perfect agreement: every one of us is broke. Debt is a cause for revolt, I'm told, and I'd love to see the two of you who are clean enough to cast the first stone, so please step forward. Nobody? Then the throne stays where it is, the jobs stay where they are, and Graham, your five goes in the book as owed and not forgotten. Lovely thing to own, an empire. Lovely thing to owe.
Tax 40%, raising nothing. No public work: the crown is in debt and can't pay toward one (320 still owed). Rob keeps the jobs; Graham's 5 goes unpaid this year.

Rob's line suggests only players out of debt could revolt. The rule (Section 16): being in debt doesn't stop a player revolting or agreeing to a revolt; the player in debt may be the one who revolts, and two other players must agree a cause exists.

The Jar, at two. Nobody can bid, so it'll come back to me, and that's fine, because it's the only thing I've got left. Rob, I heard the rule just as you did. A cause exists. I'm not calling it this year, and I'm saying so in front of everyone so it goes in the book as well.
Graham puts up the Dragon Jar, minimum 2. Nobody may bid, so it stays in his stock.

The Brush at two. Nobody can bid, so it comes back to me, and that's fine. Now look at the bank, because I'm the one holding it. Every seat at this table owes the pile, the crown can't lay a stone, and the works are still three hundred and twenty short. I'm sixty-seven down and I'm not too proud to say it: this China is finished. I propose we give up under Section 18, collapse and no winners, so nobody walks off with a throne they got by being the last one to drown. Graham, Paddy, Rob, Reina, that's my proposal. If you vote no, tell me which of you thinks this sum ever comes right.

Silke puts up the Bamboo Brush, minimum 2; nobody may bid, and it stays in her stock. Silke proposes that the table give up (Section 18): the game would end now in collapse, with no winners. The table stops only if every player agrees; each player answers in turn.

Yes, Silke. I've done the sum three times on the back of my hand and it never comes out. I'm fifty-seven and a half down, and my fields eat forty-five more than they grow every year. Nobody wins a race when we're all at the bottom of the river. If anyone votes no, the Vase is up at two, and it'll be up at two in the open every year until somebody can pay for it. That's a promise, and you all know what my promises are worth, for better or worse.
Paddy votes yes to giving up (Silke and Paddy so far). If the game goes on, he puts up the Vase, minimum 2, which nobody may bid on.

Silke, I've been doing that sum since Year 1, and I've never once had to lie to myself about it. My desert eats thirty more than it grows, my lads can't steal a piece nobody owns, and the crown can't lay a single stone. Yes. Rob, darling, the minutes can show that the last thing this table agreed on was the truth.
Reina votes yes to giving up (Silke, Paddy and Reina so far). If the game goes on, her three soldiers stand still.

Fair cop on the rule, Storyteller, I was hoping nobody would read Section 16 that closely. Silke, I've done your sum too, and the throne eats eighty-five more than it grows, which is more than any of you, so the villain votes yes. Let the minutes show that the committee finally agreed on something, and it was that I'd won a country with nothing left in it. Lovely thing to own, an empire. Lovely thing to lose. I just never thought we'd all be losing it together.
Rob votes yes to giving up. Silke, Paddy, Reina and Rob have said yes; Graham answers last.

Yes. I was one Vase short of the throne with exactly twenty in hand, and the weather took all of it in one card, so I won't pretend there's a sum here that comes right. For the minutes, Rob: everyone at this table kept their word to me this year. I didn't expect to write that twice.

Graham votes yes. Every player agrees: the table gives up in Year 8, and the game ends in collapse (Section 18), with no winners. 320 of the 520 grain of works were still owed. Final seats: Rob Emperor (drew the Warlord), Graham Silk (drew Wheat), Silke Rice (drew Silk), Paddy Wheat (drew Rice), Reina Warlord (drew the Emperor). Final grain, all in debt: Reina -5, Graham -12, Rob -45, Paddy -57.5, Silke -67.

Well, that's China done, and I'd like the minutes to show that the last Emperor's only public work was Silke's canal, and it was the only thing on this board still paying anyone at the end. Graham, your five is still in the book, and Reina, you were right: you built me a lovely house, and I couldn't afford the street. Same time next week? I'll bring the biscuits and none of you will have to pay tax on them.

Twelve down, and the second-least in debt at a table where nobody won. I've had four seats in eight years, and each one cost less than the last, until the last one cost everything. Thank you all. I'm keeping the Jar.

Then the bank closes its books. Sixty-seven down, one Brush nobody ever needed at the right moment, and every one of you kept your word to me at the very end. Rob, write it in the minutes: the Rice Peasant called time, and nobody at this table argued with the sum.

Well, there it is. Five of us went down together, and every one of us told the truth on the way. Graham, the Vase was always going to be yours at a fair price. I'm sorry the weather got to the auction before you did. Thanks for a grand game, all of you. I'll buy the tea, as soon as I'm out of the red.

Two palaces, three canals and a desert full of soldiers with nothing left to steal. Rob, darling, I built you a lovely house, and in the end none of us could pay for the street. Thank you, all of you. It was the best-run collapse I've ever had the honour to sit through.
For the record: Graham held two seats, the Wheat Peasant's from the start and the Silk Peasant's from Year 6.
